rows.evidence: Q1: Sec 2.1 - cross-sectional household survey of 383 farmers (195 MI, 187 control) in four Tanzanian districts, Feb-Mar 2021, plus qualitative interviews. Q2: Sec 3.2 and Table 3 - MI (drip-kit) farmers had higher yields, revenue and gross margins than control farmers for nearly all vegetables in Hai, Kasulu and Kilosa; Sec 3.3 - half of MI respondents used increased income for school expenses; Sec 3.7/Conclusions - MI increased income and improved livelihoods. Q3: Sec 2.1 - exploratory sequential mixed-methods design combining quantitative survey (gross margin/partial budgeting) with qualitative interviews exploring reasons for differences; Sec 3.3 interview findings on school spending, livestock and land purchases. Q4: Figures 3-8, Table 3 - yield, revenue, variable costs and gross margin per bed measured as the pathway from kits to income; Sec 3.2.4 notes yield gains and unit price drive GM. Q5: Table 1, Figures 3-8, Tables 8, A1-A4 - four districts in four regions (Manyara, Kilimanjaro, Kigoma, Morogoro) with results reported separately per district. Q6: Sec 2.1/3.2 - results aggregated across ~50 farms per district and reported at district level. Q7: Sec 3.2.4 - a higher per-unit price is vital to increase gross margin; Sec 3.7 - continued high yields not guaranteed without soil nutrient analysis; Conclusions - MI more effective when combined with market linkages assuring reasonable prices. Q8: Sec 4 - cross-sectional snapshot design a key limitation; Sec 3.4 - no baseline poverty data, possible spillover to controls; Sec 3.7 - average participation only 12 months. Q9: Figures 3-8 - standard error of mean as error bars; Tables 2, 4, 8 - means with SD.
rows.notes: The passage claims enhanced livelihoods, which the study supports via higher gross margins/income and interview reports; however the study explicitly found no significant difference between MI and control farmers on poverty, food security or asset indices overall (Tables 4, 7), with mixed district-level results (negative in Kasulu). The review's function field is 'social_cohesion', but the study reports nothing on social cohesion; it only addresses income, poverty indicators, food security and women's autonomy. Q3 triangulation rests on survey economics plus qualitative interviews, both self-reported from the same population; Q6 is at district/farm aggregation level, not scheme or basin.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey of NCA micro-investment drip kit adopters versus controls in Tanzania; economic results favor MI farmers but multivariate poverty analysis is largely null.
